description: Collectivisation, the Ukrainian famine and the Five Year Plans that industrialised the USSR.
content_html:
Why Did Stalin Collectivise Agriculture?

In 1928 the Soviet Union was still largely a peasant country. Most farming was done on small private plots by millions of individual families. Stalin believed this was economically inefficient and politically dangerous: independent farmers — especially the better-off peasants known as kulaks — could hoard grain, resist state price controls and undermine the revolution. To industrialise rapidly, the state needed to control food production and extract a surplus to feed urban workers and pay for imported machinery.

The answer was collectivisation: forcing peasants to merge their private land and livestock into large collective farms, called kolkhozy, run by the state. Stalin launched this policy in 1929, initially pushing for “voluntary” collectivisation but quickly turning to compulsion when peasants resisted.

Key Fact

Collectivisation began in earnest in 1929. By 1936 over 90 per cent of Soviet farmland had been collectivised. The policy aimed to make agriculture more efficient, give the state control over food supplies and free up labour for industrial cities.

Dekulakisation

Alongside collectivisation, Stalin launched dekulakisation — the deliberate destruction of the kulak class. Hundreds of thousands of kulak families were deported to remote regions of Siberia and Central Asia. Historians estimate that around 1.8 million people were deported in 1930–31 alone, though totals across the whole campaign were far higher. Many did not survive.

In practice, “kulak” became an elastic label applied to anyone who resisted collectivisation, hid grain or spoke against the policy. Poor peasants denounced better-off neighbours to settle old scores. The result was the destruction of the most productive section of the peasant farming community — people with the most experience and capital — at the very moment when agriculture needed their skills.

The most catastrophic consequence of collectivisation was the famine of 1932–33. Grain requisition quotas were maintained even as harvests collapsed; peasants who hid food or failed to meet quotas faced imprisonment. Ukraine, one of the Soviet Union's most fertile regions, was particularly hard hit. Historians estimate that between 3.5 and 7 million people died in Ukraine alone during this famine — known in Ukrainian as the Holodomor (literally “death by starvation”).

The Soviet government denied the famine was happening and prevented outside journalists from reporting on it. Whether the famine was a deliberate act of genocide against the Ukrainian nation or the catastrophic result of reckless policy is still debated by historians. Ukraine and many international bodies now recognise it as genocide; other historians argue the famine affected many Soviet peoples, not only Ukrainians.

The Five Year Plans

While collectivisation transformed the countryside, the Five Year Plans were transforming Soviet industry. The First Five Year Plan (1928–32) set enormous targets for coal, steel, electricity and oil production. The Second Five Year Plan (1933–37) continued industrial expansion while also developing railways and communications.

The results were remarkable by any measure. Steel production rose from around 4 million tonnes in 1928 to around 18 million tonnes by 1940. The USSR built entirely new industrial cities. The most famous was Magnitogorsk in the southern Urals — built from nothing by tens of thousands of workers, many of them deported kulaks or gulag prisoners, to become one of the world's largest steel plants. American engineers who visited in the early 1930s described it as extraordinary.

Key Fact

The Five Year Plans turned the USSR from a predominantly agricultural country into a major industrial power within a decade. Steel, coal, electricity and oil production all increased dramatically. This industrial base proved crucial in the war against Germany after 1941.

To motivate workers to exceed their targets, the state created the Stakhanovite movement, named after Alexei Stakhanov, a miner who reportedly cut 102 tonnes of coal in a single shift in August 1935 — many times the normal quota. Stakhanovites were held up as heroes and rewarded with better pay, apartments and medals. The movement created competitive pressure across workplaces but also resentment, as ordinary workers found their quotas raised to match the record-breakers.

Working conditions in Soviet industry were often dangerous and poorly paid. Managers who failed to meet targets faced accusations of sabotage — a serious charge that could lead to arrest. Workers who were persistently late or absent were dismissed and could lose their right to food rations. The combination of incentive and coercion characterised Soviet workplace culture throughout the Stalin era.

Women in Soviet Society

One notable feature of the Stalinist economy was the large-scale entry of women into industrial work. By the late 1930s, women made up roughly 40 per cent of the Soviet industrial workforce — far higher than in most Western countries at the time. Women worked in factories, on construction sites, as engineers and doctors. The Soviet state presented this as evidence of communist gender equality.

In reality, women also continued to bear the main burden of domestic work and childcare. The state provided nurseries and canteens in industrial cities, but provision was often inadequate. Women's entry into the workforce was driven less by ideological commitment to equality and more by the desperate need for labour in a rapidly industrialising economy.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Explain a Consequence’ questions on collectivisation, think beyond the immediate human cost and consider longer-term effects: for example, the destruction of experienced kulak farmers reduced long-term agricultural productivity. For ‘Explain Change’ questions on the Soviet economy, show that change was uneven — industry grew dramatically but living standards for many peasants and workers remained low. In 16-mark Period Essays, remember to weigh factors rather than just describe them.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Collectivisation (from 1929) merged peasant farms into state-controlled collectives. Dekulakisation destroyed the wealthier peasant class, and the resulting Holodomor famine killed millions in Ukraine in 1932–33.
  • The Five Year Plans drove rapid industrialisation: steel, coal and oil production grew dramatically, and new industrial cities like Magnitogorsk were built from scratch.
  • The Stakhanovite movement promoted record-breaking workers as models; women entered the industrial workforce in large numbers, though equality in practice remained limited.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Soviet collectivisation in the early 1930s.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks. Candidates may refer to: peasant farms were forcibly merged into state-controlled collective farms (kolkhozy); resistance by kulaks was met with deportation or execution; grain was requisitioned by the state even when harvests failed.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: clear feature with developed explanation.
Secure: feature identified with basic explanation.
Developing: feature stated but not developed.
Emerging: vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Five Year Plans introduced from 1928.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature (1 for identification, 1 for development). Candidates may include: ambitious state targets for heavy industries such as steel, coal and electricity; new industrial cities like Magnitogorsk were built from nothing; workers faced pressure through the Stakhanovite movement; women entered industrial work in large numbers.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: two features both fully developed.
Secure: two features, at least one developed.
Developing: two features identified but neither developed.
Emerging: only one feature, or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the Ukrainian Holodomor famine of 1932–33.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates should identify a cause and explain why it led to the famine. Strong answers show causal reasoning. Key cause: the state maintained grain requisition quotas even as harvests collapsed; peasants who hid food were arrested; the destruction of kulak farmers through dekulakisation removed the most experienced producers.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: precise cause identified, causal chain explained, specific knowledge.
Secure: cause identified and explained with relevant knowledge.
Developing: cause identified but explanation is descriptive.
Emerging: simple point with no causal reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Stakhanovite movement for Soviet industrial development.
practice_questions.marks:
Top-band answers address significance at the time AND over time. At the time: the movement created competitive pressure, raised production targets across industries and provided a mechanism for motivating workers without relying purely on coercion. Over time: it became a model for Soviet propaganda showing the 'new Soviet worker'; however, raising quotas increased resentment and may have encouraged falsification of production statistics.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: significance at time and over time, precise knowledge, sustained analysis.
Secure: significance in two ways or at two points, relevant knowledge.
Developing: significance at one point.
Emerging: description without significance judgement.

practice_questions.text:
The following is an interpretation of Stalinist economic policy:

“The suffering caused by collectivisation and the Five Year Plans was an unavoidable price to pay for transforming the Soviet Union into an industrial power.”

How far do you agree with this interpretation? Use your knowledge of Soviet history in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Candidates must agree AND disagree and reach a substantiated judgement.

Agreement: the USSR was transformed from an agricultural backwater into the world's second largest industrial economy within a decade; the industrial base built in the 1930s proved vital in defeating Germany after 1941; without collectivisation the state could not have fed urban industrial workers.

Disagreement: the Holodomor killed millions unnecessarily — the terror-famine was a policy choice, not an inevitability; dekulakisation destroyed experienced farmers, reducing long-term agricultural productivity; other paths to industrialisation (such as the NEP) existed; living standards for many workers remained very low.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: balanced argument, precise evidence, substantiated conclusion.
Secure: both sides covered, conclusion reached.
Developing: one-sided or conclusion absent.
Emerging: descriptive, no analytical engagement.

practice_questions.text: Was collectivisation more important than the Five Year Plans in transforming the Soviet economy under Stalin? Use your knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band requires a substantiated overall judgement weighing the two factors.

For collectivisation: provided the food surplus and labour force needed for industrialisation; but caused enormous human suffering and long-term damage to Soviet agriculture.

For the Five Year Plans: directly produced the industrial growth that made the USSR a major power; transformed specific sectors (steel, coal, electricity) with measurable results.

Strongest answers note that the two policies were interdependent: collectivisation was intended to supply the industrial plans.

StudyVault rubric:
Mastering: sustained argument weighing both factors, clear judgement with evidence.
Secure: two factors explained, conclusion reached.
Developing: factors listed, limited weighing.
Emerging: one factor or descriptive throughout.

knowledge_checks.q: What term describes the policy of merging peasant farms into state-controlled collective farms?
Magnitogorsk was a new industrial city built to produce which commodity?
The Ukrainian famine of 1932-33, caused by grain requisitioning, is known in Ukrainian as the _____.
Alexei Stakhanov was celebrated as a model Soviet worker in 1935 after reportedly mining a huge amount of _____ in one shift.
Match each term to its correct definition:
right: Wealthier peasants targeted for destruction during collectivisation
A state economic plan setting industrial production targets

flashcard_questions.a: Wealthier peasants who owned land or hired labour; made class enemies by Stalin.
The Ukrainian famine of 1932-33 caused by Soviet grain requisitioning.

flashcard_questions.q: Approximately how many people died in Ukraine during the 1932-33 famine?
When did the First Five Year Plan begin?
What metal was the new city of Magnitogorsk, built from scratch in the southern Urals, designed to produce?
flashcard_questions.a: Steel — Magnitogorsk became one of the world's largest steel plants.
A miner celebrated in 1935 for reportedly cutting 102 tonnes of coal in one shift.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Stakhanovite movement encourage Soviet workers to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Exceed production quotas and compete for record output.

flashcard_questions.q: By the late 1930s, roughly what proportion of the Soviet industrial workforce were women?
What happened to kulaks who resisted collectivisation?
flashcard_questions.a: They were deported to Siberia, imprisoned or executed.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the main aim of the Five Year Plans?
flashcard_questions.a: Rapid industrialisation of the Soviet economy, especially heavy industry.

glossary_terms.definition: Wealthier peasants in Russia who owned land, animals or hired labour; targeted for destruction by Stalin during collectivisation.
Stalin's policy from 1929 of merging millions of individual peasant farms into large, state-controlled collective farms.
Stalin's campaign from 1929 to destroy the kulak class through deportation, execution and imprisonment.
The Ukrainian word for the Great Famine of 1932-33, in which millions died as a result of Soviet grain requisitioning policies.
A series of ambitious state economic plans introduced by Stalin from 1928, setting targets for rapid industrial growth in coal, steel, electricity and machinery.
A new Soviet industrial city built in the southern Urals from 1929 to produce steel, symbolising the ambitions of the Five Year Plans.
Workers celebrated as models of Soviet productivity after miner Alexei Stakhanov reportedly mined 102 tonnes of coal in a single shift in 1935.
